title: Separated rotary file in the apical third of a mandibular molar MB canal
summary: F2 separated 3 mm from the apex in a curved MB canal. Retrieved under microscope with a staging platform plus ultrasonic loosening rather than bypassing.
presentation: 38-year-old female, previously initiated therapy elsewhere, presenting with intermittent pain on the lower left. Radiograph showed a radiopaque object in the apical third of the mesiobuccal canal of 36 with an intact apical seal.
unusual: The curvature was roughly 35 degrees and the fragment was engaged below the curve, so straight-line access to the fragment head was not achievable with conventional trepanning.
resolution: Removed the existing coronal restoration and re-established straight-line access under 16x magnification.
Created a staging platform with a modified Gates-Glidden #3 to expose the fragment head.
Loosened the fragment with an ultrasonic tip (dry field, intermittent 10-second bursts to avoid heat).
Fragment floated coronally in irrigant and was retrieved with a microtube plus wedge from the retrieval kit.
Completed shaping to F3, obturated with warm vertical compaction.
outcome: 6-week review asymptomatic, no periapical change. Full coverage crown planned.
takeaways: Do not attempt to bypass below a 30-degree-plus curve before creating a staging platform — the perforation risk is materially higher.
Intermittent ultrasonic bursts in a dry field give better tactile feedback than continuous activation under irrigant.

comments.author: Dr. Nikhil Menon
comments.text: Did you consider a bypass with an 08 C-file first? Curious how much dentine the staging platform cost you.

comments.author: Dr. Aparna Rao
comments.text: I tried briefly — no purchase. Platform cost maybe 0.5 mm of radicular dentine, which I judged acceptable versus the perforation risk.

title: Sinus membrane perforation during lateral window lift — managed in the same visit
summary: 8 mm perforation over an underlying antral septum. Repaired with a folded collagen membrane and grafted the same day instead of aborting.
presentation: 61-year-old male, edentulous maxillary posterior, residual ridge height 3.5 mm. CBCT showed an Underwood septum not initially appreciated on the panoramic view.
unusual: The septum divided the antral floor into two compartments; elevation from a single window tore the membrane over the septal crest.
resolution: Stopped elevation immediately and irrigated to define the perforation margins.
Extended the window mesially to gain access to the second compartment and reduce tension on the torn membrane.
Elevated remaining membrane circumferentially so the tear was fully mobilised rather than tented.
Placed a resorbable collagen membrane folded double over the defect, tucked 3 mm beyond all margins.
Grafted with particulate xenograft at low pressure, closed primarily, staged implants at 7 months.
outcome: No sinusitis, graft consolidated. Two implants placed at 7 months with 35 Ncm insertion torque.
takeaways: Always read the CBCT axial slices for septa — panoramic reconstruction hides them.
A perforation over a septum is usually salvageable if you extend the window rather than fight the tear through the original one.

comments.author: Dr. Sara Lindqvist
comments.text: Did you cover with antibiotics beyond the standard regimen?

title: Persistent pain after apparently ideal RCT — missed second mesiobuccal canal (MB2)
summary: Radiographically clean RCT on a maxillary first molar with persistent bite tenderness for 5 months. Small-FOV CBCT revealed an untreated MB2.
presentation: 44-year-old male, RCT on 16 completed 5 months earlier, well-condensed on PA. Localised tenderness to percussion, no swelling, no sinus tract.
unusual: The MB2 orifice was completely covered by a dentinal shelf and invisible even at 16x before troughing.
resolution: Small-FOV CBCT confirmed a separate untreated canal in the mesiobuccal root.
Removed the coronal restoration, dye-stained the pulpal floor to map the developmental groove.
Troughed 2 mm along the groove palatally from MB1 with an ultrasonic tip until the orifice was located.
Negotiated with a 10 K-file, shaped to 25/.04, disinfected with passive ultrasonic irrigation.
Obturated all four canals, cuspal-coverage restoration placed.
outcome: Asymptomatic at 3 months. Percussion tenderness resolved within 2 weeks.
takeaways: Percussion tenderness with a radiographically clean RCT on an upper molar should raise MB2 suspicion before you consider surgery or extraction.
Dye staining the pulpal floor is a 60-second step that repeatedly finds what magnification alone misses.

title: Buccal plate fracture during upper premolar extraction with a thin ridge
summary: Thin buccal plate fractured on luxation. Converted to socket preservation immediately to protect a planned implant site.
presentation: 52-year-old female, non-restorable 24 with a planned implant. CBCT buccal plate thickness measured 0.6 mm.
unusual: Plate fractured despite atraumatic technique — the root had a buccal concavity that effectively made the plate a shell.
resolution: Retrieved the fractured plate fragment and preserved it in saline.
Completed the extraction with vertical-only forces using physics forceps.
Repositioned the fragment, stabilised with allograft particulate and a collagen plug.
Free gingival graft for soft-tissue closure; delayed implant to 5 months.
outcome: Ridge width maintained at 6.2 mm at 5 months; implant placed without additional grafting.
takeaways: Measure buccal plate thickness on CBCT before any extraction in a planned implant site — under 1 mm, plan for preservation from the start.
Vertical-only extraction forces on thin-plate premolars; no buccal luxation.

title: Repeated anesthesia failure on an acutely inflamed mandibular molar
summary: Three failed IANBs on an irreversible pulpitis case. Achieved profound anesthesia with a buffered supplemental approach plus intraosseous injection.
presentation: 29-year-old male, spontaneous throbbing pain on 37, positive to cold, tender to percussion. Lip numb after IANB but pulp still responsive.
unusual: Lip numbness present — so the block worked anatomically — but pulpal anesthesia repeatedly failed, consistent with peripheral nociceptor sensitisation.
resolution: Confirmed soft-tissue anesthesia, then gave a buccal infiltration of 4% articaine with epinephrine.
Supplemented with an intraosseous injection distal to 37.
Tested with cold before starting; still mildly responsive, so added an intrapulpal injection after initial access.
Completed pulpectomy in the same visit with no pain reported.
outcome: Comfortable throughout; obturated at second visit.
takeaways: Lip numbness is not a test of pulpal anesthesia — always cold-test before access.
Escalate deliberately: infiltration, then intraosseous, then intrapulpal, rather than repeating the block.

comments.author: Dr. Tom Achebe
comments.text: Buffering made the biggest difference for me too. Onset drops to about two minutes.

title: Peri-implantitis with 4 mm bone loss treated by reconstructive approach
summary: Circumferential 4 mm defect around a 6-year-old implant. Surface decontamination plus reconstruction rather than explantation.
presentation: 58-year-old female, bleeding and 7 mm probing depth around a mandibular first molar implant, suppuration, implant not mobile.
unusual: The defect was contained and circumferential — an unusually favourable morphology that made reconstruction viable where most similar depths get explanted.
resolution: Full-thickness flap, granulation tissue removal, defect morphology assessed as contained on all four walls.
Mechanical decontamination with a titanium brush, then Er:YAG laser at 100 mJ / 10 Hz.
Grafted with xenograft, covered with a resorbable membrane, primary closure without implant submersion.
Systemic antibiotics 7 days, chlorhexidine rinse 2 weeks, no loading change.
outcome: 12-month probing depth 3 mm, no bleeding, radiographic fill of approximately 3 mm.
takeaways: Defect morphology, not absolute bone loss, is the main predictor of whether reconstruction will hold.
A contained circumferential defect is worth attempting to reconstruct before considering explantation.

title: Lingual nerve paresthesia after third molar surgery — recovery timeline and management
summary: Altered lingual sensation after a distoangular 48 removal. Documented the monitoring protocol and full recovery at 14 weeks.
presentation: 24-year-old female, distoangular impacted 48 with lingual angulation of the crown. Reported altered taste and numbness on the left tongue on day 1.
unusual: Sensory change without any lingual flap having been raised — attributed to retraction pressure rather than direct transection.
resolution: Documented the affected area with a mapped diagram and two-point discrimination at each visit.
Started a short high-dose steroid course within 48 hours of onset.
Reviewed at 2, 6, 10 and 14 weeks with mapped sensory testing rather than subjective report alone.
Counselled the patient explicitly on the expected recovery window and referral threshold at 3 months.
outcome: Complete resolution by week 14. No surgical exploration required.
takeaways: Map and measure sensory deficits at every visit — subjective report alone makes it impossible to tell recovery from adaptation.
Set a referral threshold in advance (commonly 3 months) so the decision is not made ad hoc.

title: Debonding aligner attachments repeatedly on a bruxist patient
summary: Attachments failed three times in six weeks. Root cause was isolation, not the composite — moving to rubber dam solved it.
presentation: 35-year-old male in aligner therapy, heavy bruxism, attachments on 14/15/24/25 debonded repeatedly, stalling tracking.
unusual: The failure was reproducible on the same four teeth only — pointing to a technique variable rather than patient load.
resolution: Reviewed bonding protocol; identified sulcular moisture contamination on the premolars with cotton-roll isolation only.
Re-bonded under rubber dam with a fresh universal adhesive and a filled flowable.
Extended cure time to 40 seconds per attachment surface.
Fitted a nightguard for use over aligners during the retention phase.
outcome: No further debonds over the following 5 months; tracking recovered without a refinement scan.
takeaways: Repeated failure on the same teeth is nearly always a technique or isolation variable, not the material.
Rubber dam for attachment bonding costs three minutes and removes the most common failure cause.
